utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Everyone can hear me, loud and clear? Interpreters up and at it? Fine. Good morning to you as well. I suggest we resume our proceedings with our fifth witness this week; is that right, counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. The Prosecution's first witness this morning is also a witness whose name appears on the inventory of witnesses, dated 16th February. He is witness number 5 on that inventory. In respect of that witness, too, your Honours, I am seeking the indulgence of the court to afford protective measures. I am seeking, your Honours, that the witness be assigned a pseudonym and that he be known as Witness C and also that the court be pleased to grant him facial image distortion during the course of his testimony. I understand my learned friend, counsel for the Defence, has no objection to my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, can you go along with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. We do not have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. So, we will take the appropriate measures to provide the said protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought I might just mention something in relation to the number of witnesses that are seeking protective measures. I thought it -- in some cases it is not as common for witnesses to seek it, but in this case, it is particularly so, having regard to the area where the witnesses are coming from. Your Honours maybe aware that under the Dayton Agreement and under the pursuance of the parties, the attitude of the government of Bosnia Herzegovina is, where possible, people should return to the areas they have come from. A lot of the people went to Zenica and the intention is that they will go back. Because of the tensions that were there and the hostilities that occurred, there is great fear by the people of going back to the community. That is why there has been so many applications in this case. We are grateful for Mr. Mikulicic's consideration of the position in regard to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel. Also thank you to counsel for the Defence for your understanding and cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, when the next witness comes, if we do not want his identity to be ascertained by his date of birth, just find out how old he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please read out the solemn declaration that the usher is handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to speak into the microphone so that everyone can hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Just read it out, standing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. Thank you very much for being here this morning. You are now going to answer the questions which the counsel for the Prosecution is going to be putting to you. WITNESS C

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I do not want to disclose your name and your personal details, details of identity and the details of where you come from. I am tendering to you a sheet of paper on which your name is written. I ask you to look at the sheet of paper and confirm whether the name on the sheet is your name. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Can it be shown to learned counsel for the Defence, and your Honours. (Handed). My Lords, I am tendering this sheet with the name of the witness as an exhibit. Thank you, your Honours. Witness, you are Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you tell this court what your age is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you recall the 27th day of January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: On that day, where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at my home. I was supposed to have dinner together with the rest of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you when you were at home that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what happened to you that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers arrived in the village and they took myself, my neighbours and my son. They searched the village and they took us forcibly to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How did you know that those soldiers who arrived in the village were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing insignia, "HVO" insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What type of uniform were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how many soldiers -- do you recall about how many soldiers came to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between eight and ten. It was dark and we were supposed to leave our homes with our hands behind our necks, so we were not -- we could not look around. We were lined up against a wall and the six of us -- five of my neighbours and myself -- this is how we were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Altogether six of you were taken with your hands behind your neck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Busovaca, to the police station and we simply stood there for a while. We were still on the bus. From there we left by bus to the bus station in Busovaca. Then we were told to go out, to get out, to get off the bus and to stand against the wall, and our hands were still behind our necks. After we got out, we were lined up against a wall and at that moment a truck arrived, an FUT truck which had an anti-aircraft machine gun mounted on it. The crew got out and started beating us and that is when I sustained most of my injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who were the members who got out of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were beaten badly on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were the other five members of your village also beaten by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were, but I was the one who received most blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when you were beaten, did anybody intervene at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one of the HVO soldiers, the one who had taken us from the village and who was escorting us, did intervene, but it was too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And where were you beaten? On which part of your body were you mostly beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was hit in the back and my spine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you still suffer from those beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened thereafter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers forced us on the bus again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After being forced into the bus, what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started out in the direction of Smreka, in the direction of the building called the 11 Plavih.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did the bus stop at the 11 Plavih building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who accompanied you to the 11 Plavih building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened when the bus stopped at 11 Plavih building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point we were ordered to get off the bus and then they started searching us. They found a small calendar on me, which had a "BiH" sign imprinted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What happened when they found the calendar on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Popovic, nicknamed Isus, he forced me to eat the calendar. I had to eat it because he was ready to hit me. I was terribly afraid and I think I urinated a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The calendar you referred to is a pocket calendar, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a small plastic calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you beaten on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we got off the bus, they carried out the search and after I had eaten the calendar, we were forced to go into the building, the 11 Plavih building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, what happened as you were going into the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same soldier was there again. We could not simply enter the building, we were supposed to pass between two rows of soldiers and nobody could pass through that row without being hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In what position were you taken when you entered the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand your question. What do you mean by "position"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you walked into that building, were you forced to keep your hands behind your neck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said several times, all the way from the house to the prison, we had to keep our hands behind our necks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what happened when you went to the 11 Plavih building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same HVO soldiers ordered us to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you sit down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We had to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you see other people in the 11 Plavih restaurant when you went in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw some civilians, Muslim civilians from Busovaca and also some people from the village of Prosje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: For how long were you inside the 11 Plavih building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you exactly for how long because we were afraid. It was dark, it was night-time and there were many provocation. It was difficult really to hold out, but I think we were kept there for about one hour or two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And did anything happen to you whilst you were inside the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but there were lots of provocations and lots of mistreatment, you know, all the bad things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You mean there were lots of verbal mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After being in the building for about an hour or two, could you tell this court what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same HVO soldiers, including Ivan Popovic, who was there all the time, they ordered us back into the bus. After we left the 11 Plavih building the procedure was the same again, we had to run the gauntlet and nobody could pass through it without being hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you and your colleagues got into the bus, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it only the six of you from your village who were brought in the bus or were there others brought as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were others as well, people whom we had found in the 11 Plavih building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were brought to Kaonik; where in Kaonik were you brought to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the camp, to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was this camp before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It used to be a warehouse that belonged to the former JNA. There were several depots there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you tell this court what happened upon reaching the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ordered us to get off the bus and enter the camp. They took down our personal details when we were already in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to show an exhibit to the witness. With your permission, the usher would be pleased to show an exhibit to the witness, and there are copies for your Honours as well as a copy for the learned Defence counsellor. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit number 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please -- usher, could you please place the photograph on the ELMO? Witness, could you look at the photograph on the ELMO and tell the court at which point you got off the bus in the Kaonik camp premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on map). The bus brought us here. This is where we got off the bus, here, at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Having got --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in front of this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you got off the bus in front of that building, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to one of the prison buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you identify which prison building you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To this one here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Please could you encircle that building with the highlighter that is on the table and mark it with the letter "A"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Because I was kept in two buildings, I was first taken to this one, then I was transferred to another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Of those two, which one were you first taken to? Could you place the letter "A" on the building to which you were first taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Then you said -- from there you said you were put into the next building which you have marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after about 10 days, we were transferred to another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you mark that building with the letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that upon arrival in the first building, on arrival at the camp, your personal details were taken down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who took down your personal details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was this man with very fair complexion and blond hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was an official there. He was supposed to take down our details, the details from all persons detained in the camp. He was also wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were the details of the others who were brought taken down as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After your details were taken down -- personal details were taken down, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me to a cell, together with my son, Hamid, and others were taken to other cells. The cells were crowded so we could not fit into one, so they sent, for example, two of us into one cell and then three or four others to another, depending on how crowded the cell already was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: In the cell into which you and your son were put, about how many were there already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was pretty crowded. Maybe 18 persons, so we were between 18 and 20 inside the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you describe the cell to which you were put in that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? What kind of description do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Describe the cell and the conditions within the cell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were very bad. It was an untenable situation in the cell. The Kaonik prison had been established only recently and the work was not completed yet. There were some wooden planks that were put on the cement floor. There was some straw on the floor, some military clothing that used to belong to the former JNA, the clothing was left in one of the warehouses, and we also had a blanket or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was there any heating in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no light at all. We did not have any light in the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: About how long did you spend in this particular cell that you were first put into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to say because it was so painful and I was afraid, so I cannot tell you the exact number of days I spent there. Between seven or ten days maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During the time that you spent in the cell, were you able to hear or observe what was happening in the building outside -- within the building, outside your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every evening we could hear, and that was the most difficult thing to bear for me, because I had been badly beaten and I could not sleep at all and we did not even have enough room to lie down, so I would simply sit down, lean next to one of my colleagues. So I kept listening to those cries and moans coming from the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what time -- you said you heard them mostly because you could not sleep in the nights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: At any point in time were you taken out of your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never taken out of my cell for beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: But were you taken out for anything else, other than beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, only to get some food for lunch and for dinner. Only then were we taken out. Also when we wanted to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were suffering from great pain as a result of the beatings. What did you do about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I requested to be taken to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were you taken to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the health centre at Busovaca, which was controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you given any treatment at the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really say that it was any help at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After you were brought back from the health centre were you put into the same cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said you were moved from that cell into the other building, which you marked with the letter "B"; how many nights did you spend in that building, in the second building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About eight to ten days, but it was terrible. I cannot remember much because I was in a great deal of pain. Let me say something that I forgot to say a minute ago, that I slept -- I said that I had slept in the shed and fallen there, I did not say that I had actually received my injuries in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: To whom did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the doctor when I was taken to the health the centre. I said that I fell off the shed. I did not dare say that I had been beaten by the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you told an untruth for fear of the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, when you were in the camp in the cell, did you see other prisoners being taken out of their cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you cannot see from the cell. Let us get that clear. You can just hear the screams after the beatings, the thud of the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you hear the names of other prisoners being called out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was usually a roll call because lots of people were taken to do hard labour, they were taken to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During your stay in the camp, did you have occasion to see who the commander of the camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we were taken out for lunch, for food, I did, yes. Perhaps once or twice, we saw him about once or twice in passing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander of the camp was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise him if you see him today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and his picture -- I have a picture from earlier days when we were in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you look around in this court and say whether the camp commander, Zlatko Aleksovski, is present in this court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And is he the gentleman -- could you point out where he is seated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. The transcript should make clear that the witness did point towards Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that you saw him about two occasions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: During your stay in the camp, at any point of time, did the ICRC visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except the worst thing was that the register is not taken down when the prisoner is brought, but when the Red Cross comes, not before then. That is the first time they take the register, they take the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Were you visited by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ICRC visited all of us who were there. Some of us went to do the labour and when we were all collected, all there together, they would take down our particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And about how many days after your detention were you released from prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot quite answer that question exactly because I was too ill and too much afraid to remember exactly, but it was about 20 days -- some 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you know who organised the release -- who organised your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It went via the Red Cross. As far as I was able to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And upon being released, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went home, most of us returned home. In most cases we went back to our own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After your release, have you been taking treatment for the injuries caused as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I got home, because we did not have any doctor. We had to go down back to Busovaca again and Busovaca was under HVO control. So, only what we could do at home, we put balms on our wounds and some other home medicines because we had nobody to go to, or where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: After your release, did you have occasion to see Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we saw each other somewhere around July. It was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Of which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances in which you saw him in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My village was burnt on the 19th April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Mr. Mikulicic, you wanted to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting the questions by my learned colleague. I would like to answer these questions because it is a period which is not incorporated into the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, although it does not relate to the period of the indictment, I am seeking to admit the evidence for the reason that it is an item of evidence which pertains to establish the identity of the accused. For that reason, I submit that this evidence is both relevant and admissible, your Honours. Because the question at issue is also the identity of the accused. That is a vital issue that has to be established by the Prosecution, one of the limbs to be established by the Prosecution. It is my submission that this item of evidence which I intend to lead through this witness would further the issue of identity of the accused because the witness has seen the accused when he was in the camp and there was also an occasion on which the witness saw him thereafter. I must also submit that I am sure my learned friend is not taken by surprise because this is part of the statement of the witness and the statement has been disclosed to the Defence well in advance of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, two more words from me. May I say something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence in no way opposes the identification of the defendant by the witness. In that sense it is outside the time limit of the indictment and, therefore, not within procedural limits. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Chamber admits the question only for the purpose of identification of the accused. So, if it is necessary for the purpose of identification, then we can admit that question. Only for that purpose. Please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honours. Witness, you said you saw the accused thereafter in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when he came in the evening after midnight to myself and a relation of mine and when he expelled this cousin's parents from their house --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This has nothing to do with the identification of the witness, because he identified the defendant earlier on. He showed him out, pointed him out in the courtroom and the Defence has no criticisms there. It does have opposition to this description of events which step outside the time limits incorporated by the indictment. So any questions and answers of this kind we are definitely opposed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Go ahead, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not intending to elicit evidence which is going to cause prejudice to the accused. I am only getting this evidence in order to further the evidence of this witness about the identity of the accused so he corroborates himself, having seen the accused, not only within the Kaonik camp but also thereafter and today, therefore, his identity of this accused in this court today would further be strengthened as a result of this evidence. I am not for a moment relying on the actual incident that happened, but in order to establish that the accused, in fact, saw him thereafter and his identification of the accused today is a valid identification and it is for that purpose that I intend to lead this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But, counsel, are there any doubts as regards identification of the accused? I think the witness did identify the accused here in this courtroom. So, I am not sure I see the purpose you are pursuing here in terms of identification --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If my learned friend concedes the identity of the accused, in that event I will not proceed further with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, I think that the accused has been clearly identified by the witness. So I think we can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise, one more point from me. If your Honours have determined that any further description of the events is superfluous, I would like it struck from the record, what the witness said when he described events outside the time limits incorporated by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I doubt whether the witness said anything outside -- about the events outside the time frame incorporated. Before the witness could narrate the incident, my learned friend's objection was recorded and I think the witness was precluded from saying anything except that he remembers seeing the accused coming to the house that evening, sometime in July 1993. The witness has not said anything that the accused did that evening, or could not proceed to say anything about the accused, apart from the fact that he saw the accused in July 1993. Your Honours may disregard that evidence. When an assessment of the evidence is made, your Honours may disregard the evidence. I do not think at this stage there is any need to expunge or redact any material from the record, your Honours. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to go on with the testimony, leaving the statement as it stands. It is redundant, as it were, and it in no way is detrimental to the accused, so we will go on with the witness's testimony now. So please proceed, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Very well, your Honours. Your Honours, in that event, if your Honours are not expunging any answer that went down on the record, I have no further questions, your Honours, in examination-in-chief from the witness. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I take it that you would like to proceed with your cross-examination? Do go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, witness number C, I am Mr. Mikulicic, the Defence counsel for Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski. I am going to ask you several questions and would kindly ask you to answer them to the best of your ability.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am able, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, you told us in your introduction in the indictment of the events of 27th January 1993 when HVO soldiers came to your village. Could you, please, tell us now whether you know what they were looking for in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, they wanted to take us prisoner, not only myself, but everybody in the Busovaca municipality, to be locked up, was to be locked up. It was not only me, it was everybody else as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Witness C, did the soldiers search your brother's house and your house and the houses of the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they on that occasion take anything away from your brother's house or your own house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what they took from your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took a rifle and they took a hunting rifle from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of rifle did they take from your brother's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did they confiscate any weapons from your neighbours' houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened with those weapons, where were they taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken to the police station in Busovaca, HVO police station in Busovaca. When we went to the bus stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you, please, tell us, Witness C, are you a soldier -- were you a soldier or civilian at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was also a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that when you were taken to Busovaca, to the bus stop there, that you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that a man came to you -- that a man intervened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the man's name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the group that took us from the village, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name was Batinic Ivica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did Batinic Ivica intervene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he criticised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who did he criticise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers who beat us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Ivica Batinic was opposed to this to protect you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am telling the truth. I said I would tell the truth and I am telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you said that you were taken to the 11 Plavih restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, is that building in any way linked to the Kaonik buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 11 Plavih was the command of the units in Donja Polje, Smreka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is that the same territory as Kaonik or is it further off from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It belongs to the Busovaca municipality, but one is on one side of Busovaca and the other is on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three or four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were brought to Kaonik, you said that your particulars were taken there. Who did that? Who registered you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said in my statement that an elderly man who had a white pale face, he was blond. But this was in the evening, there was no light, our hands had to be behind our backs so I was not quite able to see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The man you have just described, was he one of those people who came to fetch you in your village and took you to Busovaca to the 11 Plavih building or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a man from the Kaonik camp. And I saw him later on, on several occasions, but I was not interested in knowing who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that it was one of the guards in the Kaonik building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It could only have been a warden, or an officer of the warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anybody talk to you when you came to Kaonik? Did anybody say anything to you from the camp officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Witness C, that amongst the guards in Kaonik camp you recognised some of your neighbours and acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, amongst the guards. Are you asking me amongst the guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am asking you about the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you, please, tell us who those people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know them from sight, by sight, Juresic Kebo, Sakic Ljubo. Then there was Basic, Faca was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was their conduct towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards me personally, they were correct in their conduct, and I think for the other prisoners they would have been the same, but when a smaller group of soldiers would come, they were impotent, they do nothing about it. A guard in the evening was on guard in the evening and then a bigger or smaller group would open the cells up and maltreat the inmates or curse them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why could not they stop the group doing what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were drunk, more or less. They were either drunk or they were drugged. There was a great deal of noise in the corridors, a lot of cursing going on and then if a guard was to protect him, then they would -- the mafia would beat him up too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Could you please tell us, Witness C, you described that you were injured and you said you were taken to the doctor. Who took you to the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers and my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the doctor you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, because I never used to go to doctors, to the health centre at all, so I do not know. And I was not taken on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, you did not go to the health centre very often, so you did not know the names of the people working there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but it was a man, a male doctor. I was taken to a male doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if he wrote anything down pertaining to your injuries when you were brought to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just examined me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did he write anything down, did you see him write anything down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he just told me that he -- I should be taken to a surgeon at Bila, but there were no conditions for this to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why did he say there were no conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why he said that. He did not have the facilities. He was unable to take me to Bila, to the surgeon there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that, you were taken back to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When the counsel asked you a moment ago, you said that there was no heating in the cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there any heating in the corridors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some stoves made up of some primitive stoves with primitive pipes in the corridors. Above the doors there were bars and so some heat and light came into our cells through the iron bars above the doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you were taken out of your cells for food, for lunch or dinner. Did you ever notice the guards eating together with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice where the guards took their meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because while we were eating, we were left alone, nobody was with us there. Once we had finished there, we were taken back to the cells immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness C, was there any fighting around your village at that time, any gunfire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, up above the village, and we were under the control of the HVO, my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when you say "above the village", how far was this shooting from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the fighting took place some five kilometres -- maybe 10 kilometres -- away, or not -- not less than three kilometres away, 3, 5, 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that when you came to your cell you found some old uniforms there. Could you clarify this? What kind of old uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the former JNA, Yugoslav People's Army. Coats and some of their blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you use those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we had nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who gave you those uniforms and blankets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We found them in the cells, in the rooms in the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you in that way able to keep away the cold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Witness C, I am not quite sure that I understood you correctly, so please correct me if I am wrong. You said that you had a picture of Zlatko Aleksovski, a photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that if I saw one of his photographs I would be able to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not understand you correctly, witness. Thank you for clarifying that. I think that would be all from our side. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I say a few words please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You would like to add something, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You do have something more to say, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For the conditions in the second building where we were taken to, the kind of conditions there for survival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Counsel, both for the Prosecution and the accused, do you think it would be worth hearing more on this particular point? Go ahead, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Unless the witness has something more to add -- if your Honours would permit me, I could ask the witness what he has to add about the conditions in the second building and then my learned friend may, in that event, if he wishes to, ask further questions in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence considers that the witness has already testified as to the situation in the second building. The Defence had no questions with regard to re-examination, so I do not think my learned colleague should have any questions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness C, you have now concluded with your testimony. The Chamber has been sufficiently enlightened as far as those conditions go, so we would like to thank you for having come to this court. I do not know whether you might have any questions, I do apologise? No. That is it, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you for the Prosecution, I suggest that we have a recess once Witness C has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I might suggest that all the screens and things be left in place because the next witness will be seeking protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. We are going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please the court, your Honours, the next witness has sought certain protective measures; namely, that the image of his face be distorted and that he be accorded a pseudonym rather than use his name. In his case, your Honours, might he be referred to as "Witness D"? He is the witness that appear in the inventory of witnesses as witness number 6, your Honours. We have raised the matter in correspondence with Mr. Mikulicic and we understand there is no objection to the application, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, that is fine by you, is it? Maybe you could show the witness in. First, if you would lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me, sir? Please read out the solemn declaration which the usher is giving you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please be seated. You are now going to answer the questions from the counsel for the Prosecutor's Office. WITNESS D

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, the court has afforded you certain protective measures. As a consequence of that, I will not refer to you by your name during the course of your evidence, I will refer to you as "Witness D". I ask you to look at this piece of paper which I now show you. It has written on it a name. I would ask you to look at the name that appears there -- do not say the name -- and simply tell me whether or not it is your name; "yes" or "no". (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it could be shown to Mr. Mikulicic and the bench. Your Honours, I tender that under seal. I ask you that, during the course of your evidence, you are not to refer to your current or previous address. Can you tell me how old you are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by religion, are you Islam or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In 1993, were you in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what position did you have in the army? Where were you located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On 25th or 26th January 1993, did hostilities commence in and about the area of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At about 3.00 pm in Kacuni fighting started. We happened to be in the centre of Busovaca so we did not know what was happening, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the fighting started, were you a soldier at the time? Were you defending the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the fighting started, we simply took shelter somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And where did you take shelter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to a cottage house in the vicinity of our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At that very time were you dressed in military uniform yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you carrying any arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have any weapons, the weapons were at the front-line, the front-line against the Cheekiness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there any BiH soldiers in Busovaca at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were some soldiers, but we, we did not offer any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after you took shelter? What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed in the shelter for about five or six days, until 30th January. Then after that we left home. In the morning, around 10.00 or 11.00 am HVO members arrived and they asked for weapons. They asked each of us for weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How did you know that they were HVO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit P17, if your Honours please? Witness, we will show you an exhibit now. We would like to put it on to the overhead projector there. If you would look at it for me, you might, with the pointer, point to it on the machine beside you. If you recognise any of the pictures shown, point to them on the screen if you would, please. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on picture).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might point again for us, if you would, the one that you recognise. It is upside down, but that does not matter. For the record, you are pointing to the second photograph, number 2 -- numbered "number 2". Thank you. That was the one you recognised on the uniforms of those soldiers on that occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they do? They asked you for your weapons. Did you have any weapons to surrender to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these people? Were they people that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised two of them, Dario Lastro and Marijan Varesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they all soldiers or were some other organisations represented by these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were just simple soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, after they asked you for the weapons, what did they do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not find anything and then they lined us up and we had to walk to the centre of Busovaca in a line, one by one. Then they searched us near a bus, which then took us to Kaonik, to the Kaonik prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "us", who is "us"? How would you describe "us"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 18 of us from my street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of these people, what was the ethnic background of the 18 people in the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you -- you say you went to the centre of Busovaca; how long did you stay there before you were taken to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They just carried out a search which took about five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were they looking for, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess they were looking for pistols or hand grenades, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was anything taken of you at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did all the Muslim people that were in your street go into the street and off to Kaonik or was it just some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 of us were taken there, but some elderly people had remained, maybe three or four of them, and two families remained in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when the soldiers were asking for your weapons, did they have any documents with them relating to weapons or anything of that nature that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had a kind of paper, this is probably something that they had seized in the company headquarters. It was a list of formations and units and it was a list of people issued with some kind of weapons, although we did not actually have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you specifically addressed by a soldier in relation to a weapon, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were looking for snipers, sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they suggest that you might have had a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were looking for sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say to them when they asked you for a sniper rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told them I did not have any and I also told them that weapons I had been issued were some automatic rifles but that those weapons were actually at the line, near Visoko, at the front-line near Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the afternoon, sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, are you able to remember the date, what date this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on 30th January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Kaonik, what did they do with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They through us into one of the cells, I think it was cell number 16. After that they took a roll call and they put us up in room where they carried out the interrogation. Krilic Marko and Marko Petrovic were the interrogators, they were wearing camouflage uniforms at that time. They asked us about weapons and they had that list with them. So they interrogated us for about five or ten minutes and then they took us back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you had been arrested and put in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said it was for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they suggest that you had any particular sort of weapon or was it just a general sort of question about weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked for specific weapons. Hand-held rocket launchers, M53 machine-guns, everything according to the list that had been drawn up, this is what they were looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a possession of any of these types of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, of the other prisoners that were there when you arrived, did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In cell number 16, we found two persons there, one was from Zenica and I did not know the other one -- well, I did not know the first one either, but I just happened to know that he was from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did anyone receive any beatings or anything of that nature during the period of time that this questioning went on when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in our group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the age group of the prisoners that were there in those cells, so far as you were able to ascertain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 13, 14 years old until 65 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many people were 13 years of age, or that young, that age group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was one boy who was there with us and he was between 13 and 14 years of age. He was from Prosje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then? Were the people all kept together or was there some separation process that went on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was transferred to another cell, cell number 12. Around 6.00, they through Fehim into our cell, he had been badly beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he tell you what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that HVO soldiers had beaten him. In the town. In the town of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say why he had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that there was one boy who was 13/14 years of age and that there were older men, as old as 65. Did they stay in the cells with you or were they separated out from the cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were separated on the following day. When we returned from the digging, I found some new people in the cell, the elderly men were gone. So, in my cell, there were no elderly people any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like you to look for me, if you would, at Exhibit 20, if that could be shown to the witness. Again, if it could be placed on the screen. (Handed). I understand we have some copies of that for your Honours of that photograph and Mr. Mikulicic. (Handed). Witness D, just looking at that photograph that now appears on the screen beside you there, could you, with your pointer, point to the cell that you were placed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember what number that cell was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was cell number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just for the record, your Honour, the witness has pointed to the right-hand side of the photograph, the cell door the furthest away on the right-hand side of the photograph. How long did you stay in that cell for, that you have just pointed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the interrogation, maybe for about two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And does the other cell that you were moved to, does that appear on this photograph at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you, looking at the photograph, assist us by describing the direction that the other cell was located at? I know you cannot point to it, but can you assist us in pointing to the direction of where the other cell was? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cell was located on the right side from the lavatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps with your pointer, you might point in what direction, if you were walking down the cells, which way you would find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness is pointing to the left-hand side of the photograph and coming up to the face of the photograph. Thank you, that could be returned. Now, the next day, what happened then? What happened to you on the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took a roll call in the morning; they took about 30 of us in a truck, in a civilian truck to a location called Milavice. 15 of us got off the truck at Milavice and the rest of the group continued to the Prosje location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was that boy of 13 or 14 years of age with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with us on the second or the third day, when we were at Prosje, I saw him there while we were digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you got to Milavice, what happened then, what were you required to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to dig dug-outs, we had to fix them, we had to dig communication trenches between the dug-outs. We worked until 9.00 pm without any food or water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were working in these dug-outs, did you have any notion of where the front-line was at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could only make assumptions as to where it might be, maybe 5-600 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any firing or fighting going on across the lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was some sporadic shooting, sporadic fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you given food and water and rest while you were digging these trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not get any food or water. We did have small breaks of about five or ten minutes, just enough to have a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In January, what were the conditions like for digging -- early February, I think, probably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very bad. It was cold, the earth was frozen, we were not -- we did not have warm clothes. The conditions were very bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did you work up to in the day or night, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 9.00 or maybe 10.00 pm, we worked until 9 or 10 on that first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we would go to the barracks and sleep there and the next day we were taken to dig trenches again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who called you out to dig trenches, who was it who came and told you to come out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The roll call was usually taken by Marko Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were asked to come out, where did you come out from the cell? Where did you go precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would meet in the corridor, we would wait for everybody to get out of their cells, then they would put us on to a truck and the truck would take us to the location where we were supposed to dig.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was any record kept of who was being sent and who was left behind, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, do you recall any incidents where people were injured or killed when they were taken to trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard about the killing of two persons at the Kula location, Ermin Elezovic and Jasmin Sehovic were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You never saw that yourself, you simply heard of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see that but I did see when Nedzab Delion was hit several times by an HVO member as he was getting off the truck. He was simply telling him that he should not try to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you ever see any other beatings or mistreatment of the people, of the prisoners, the detainees when you were taken trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall any incidents where detainees were forced to beat each other; did that ever happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened at Kula. We learned that when we came back, that people were forced to hit each other with shovels. It took place on 8th February, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, it is not something you, yourself, saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many places were you taken to in order to dig trenches? How many different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of those places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prosje, Milavice, Kovacevac and Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown a copy of the map. If this might be marked the next exhibit number in order. I believe there are copies there for the witness, your Honours and one for Mr. Mikulicic. (Handed). Witness D, I want you to pick up a highlighter pen -- I can see a pink highlighter pen which you have beside you, if you study that map so you are familiar with it and take your time, see if you can see on the map the places there named that you were taken to for the purposes of trench digging. When you have identified where the places are, I would like you to put it on the overhead projector before you actually mark it and mark it on the overhead projector, the plan, so we can see. Could you do that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just do it on the machine beside it and then we can all see what you are doing. Just tell us the name of the place when you are marking it, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kovacevac. Kula. But on this map, you cannot see Prosje and Milavice. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, just point -- just draw a line in the general direction, would you, of where they are, if you could just draw an arrow for us in the direction that they are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender those, your Honour, as the exhibit number in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What number might that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned that on one of the occasions you went to Prosje that the 13-year-old boy went with you. Did you actually work with him on that day, or did he work with somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He worked with his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But were they near you? Could you see them or were they separated from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were some 10 or 15 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you see them working during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the 13-year-old boy required to work under the same conditions, as you could observe, as the men were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had to do the same work as his father. They brought wood, they had to cover the dug-outs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did the Red Cross ever visit Kaonik camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, on the third or the fourth day. They made a list so we were all registered with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after you were registered with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing, we just continued with the same kind of work, we went on digging dug-outs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross say what would happen to you at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that there would be an exchange, in about a day or two, but the exchange took place only on 8th February.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you exchanged on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were exchanged on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 420 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross say anything to you about trench digging, that you can remember, or representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have to go trench digging after you had been visited by the Red Cross or did it cease then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We still had to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in the camp, can you remember? What was the food and heating and blankets and water and sanitary conditions like? Can you describe those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food was just some simply boiled food and two people had to share one plate. We could not take a bath, we could not shave ourselves. We used to sleep in the cell, 20 or 25 of us together, so there was not enough room. Some people would lie down and some people had to sit down and sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, -- when you were actually kept in the cells, do you recall any incidents of anyone being beaten or mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you hear anything going on outside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were exchanged, how many people were exchanged, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, we all left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you go after you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three options: Kacuni, Zenica and Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What option did you select?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The guards at the Kaonik prison, do you remember how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In camouflage uniforms with "HVO" insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have some questions, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to welcome you, Witness D. My name is Mr. Mikulicic, I am the Defence counsel for the defendant, Zlatko Aleksovski. I am going to ask you several questions I would like to ask you to answer to the best of your ability. Tell us, please, at the time when you were taken prisoner, what were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that the soldiers of the HVO searched the neighbourhood, searched the houses in your neighbourhood. You said that they had a list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You also said that the list was seized somewhere. Can you tell us in greater detail where this list came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the HQ, headquarters, of the company, the Busovaca HQ company's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my defendant has asked for a two-minute break for consultations with me. May this be allowed? May we just have two minutes in the courtroom, please, so that I can confer with the defendant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Do take two minutes, and only two minutes, please. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are ready to continue. May I continue with my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you said that the list that the soldiers had when they searched the houses was seized. Could you repeat where it was seized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the health centre. By the company command, from the company command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What company are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Busovaca company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To which army did it belong?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that fighting around Kacuni began in those days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of weapons were used in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not directly there, but I heard that they were the Zoljas, the hand-held launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe the kind of weapons they were? What do you mean by a "Zolja"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an anti-armoured weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe it in closer terms? It is a rocket launcher, hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who used the hand-held rocket launchers in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I was not present, I was in Busovaca at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
