utterances.text: So you do not know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the events when you were brought to Kaonik. You said that you were told you were there for safety reasons, security reasons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that explained to you by anybody, that statement, was it explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told -- we were told we were there for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure, Marko Krilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was that person a guard in Kaonik or was it an HVO soldier who took you to Kaonik; do you know who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said you were sent to the cell and that there were younger people and older people in that cell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them in Prosje. The youngest I saw in Prosje, not in the prison --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Would you repeat what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The youngest person I saw in prison, I saw in Prosje, where we dug the dug-outs. That was the youngest person that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you correctly, are you talking about the boy you mentioned earlier on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not see the boy in the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him in the cell that I was located at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you saw him on the digging site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the boy comes from, which village he is from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is from Ocehnici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his name is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know his name, but his surname is Ebric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How do you know how old he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By looking at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any document from which you were able to deduce how old he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How old would you say I was, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is the village of Ocehnici from the site where you saw that boy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The boy is from Ocehnici and the location -- the locality is about 1.5 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that he was together with his father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see his father in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you were taken from Kaonik to the localities you talked about for digging purposes, who watched over you? Who guarded you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers on the front-line, the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, if I have understood you correctly, they were not the guards from Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the commander on the Kula front-line was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us earlier on that during the time you worked in these localities, that shooting could be heard in the background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sporadic shooting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see anybody of the people who were together with you in that locality, whether they were wounded or injured by that shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see anybody wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You explained to us that you were taken to four different localities, two of which you noted on the map and two which you did not because you could not find them on the map. How far are those locations -- please enumerate them one by one -- away from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milavice and Prosje, they are about six or seven kilometres away from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Kula?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what the food was like in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was cooked food, ordinary food. Two prisoners would eat from one plate and one piece of bread would be divided between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you took your meals, in the cells or inside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see where the guards were having their meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of food the guards ate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Witness D, on 8th February 1993, you were freed, released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that was on an exchange basis or whether it was release, because you said that all the people had left Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who were you exchanged for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was exchanged with the prisoners who were in Kacuni of the Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who imprisoned these people of the Croatian nationality in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many prisoners of the Croatian nationality were released on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 30 to 40, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many prisoners were released from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all released, about 420 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that nobody remained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, we were all released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The Defence has no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So then, Witness D, you have concluded your testimony. We would like to thank you most heartily for having come before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness has also sought protective measures, similar to this witness who has just testified. The witness is seeking the image of his face not appear unless it is distorted and that he be assigned a pseudonym. In his case, it would be "Witness E", if we refer to him as that. This witness appears on your Honours' list which was filed by the Prosecutor as witness number 8. We have raised the matter with Mr. Mikulicic and, so far as we know, there is no objection to this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Counsel for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Niemann. I was just thinking that it might be good to have a 10-minute break and then we could go on non-stop until the end of today's proceedings with this witness. I think we all need a rest, including the interpreters, and I do think it might be a good time for a break. What do you think, counsel for the Prosecution and for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am in your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We agree with your suggestion, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Then during the recess, we could show the witness in and then we could get on with the questioning right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, we will arrange that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 10 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While we are waiting, at this stage, your Honours, I might indicate that witness number 7 on the list will not be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, can we have the witness brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are arranging that, your Honour. I think the staff are not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Can you hear me? Fine. Please read out the solemn declaration, which the usher is now going to hand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Please answer the questions which the counsel for the Prosecution is going to be putting to you. Mr. Niemann, please proceed. WITNESS E

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, their Honours have awarded you certain protective measures for your security. As a consequence of that, I will refer to you, in the course of your evidence, as "Witness E". When you are giving your evidence, please do not give your current or past address, during the course of the evidence. I would like you to look at the piece of paper that I now show you. This piece of paper has a name on it. If it is your name, would you say "yes" or "no", please, but do not mention the name that appears on the piece of paper. (Handed)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be shown to Mr. Mikulicic and their Honours. I tender that as the next Prosecution exhibit number in order, and might it be under seal?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution exhibit 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness E, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You might have to sit forward a little bit, just so your voice can be clearly picked up when you are answering my questions, thank you. Witness E, I would like to take you to 15th April 1993 at approximately 5.00 to 6.00 pm in the afternoon when I think at that stage you were at your home and something happened. Do you recall that date and time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 5.00 or 6.00 pm I was not exactly at my home but I was in the village and two trucks with soldiers arrived and they encircled the village. After that an HVO commander, Andrijasevic, who was in charge of the area, he ordered that all men should gather at one point for the purpose of an agreement or a meeting. We gathered there, but to no avail. Then later a smaller vehicle arrived, a van, that was driven by Mirko Plavcic and they transported us in groups to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These soldiers -- you said there was an HVO commander; were they HVO soldiers that surrounded the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore those insignias, HVO insignias on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps quickly the witness might be shown Exhibit P17. Witness E, would you look at the exhibit that you are now being shown? It is going to be placed on the overhead projector beside you. With the pointer that there is there in front of you on the table, could you point to the document that now appears on the screen? That particular photograph, if any, you recognise as being the ones worn by the soldiers on that particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we have to wait because it is not appearing on the screen, your Honours. Now, can you point to it not on the television screen but on the overhead projector beside you. The witness pointed, your Honours, to photograph number 2. Might that be now returned to the Registrar? The people that were taken to the Kaonik camp, on that occasion, who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who were taken there? Could you clarify that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who did they take to Kaonik camp on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took the people from that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these people Croats and Serbs and Muslims or was there only one particular group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One particular group, yes, they were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were -- what were the sex? Were they males and females or just males?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only males.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what was the age group of the people that were taken? What did it range from, that you can best recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It ranged from 25 or 23 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time did you arrive at the Kaonik camp, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived there, where did you go, firstly? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were first taken into the hangar. After we got in, they ordered us to press our hands against the wall and not to turn around. That is how we remained standing for about two hours, or even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who ordered you to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards who were there at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they the same people that had brought you to the camp or were they new people, so far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And were you searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They said that everything relating to the army, any documents, should be handed over to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Anything else? Was anything else taken from the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whoever had watches or gold or jewellery, that was all taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about money, was any money taken off the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they take anything off you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not take anything from me. I managed to hide it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any military papers pertaining to yourself on your possession at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have it on me because when I was arrested at home I think I was wearing a suit and my documents were not there, they were left at home, so that is how I did not have anything on me at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in the army immediately prior to your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And what position did you have in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not clear to me what exactly you mean by "position".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you on active duty on the day you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: (Question Inaudible).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And immediately prior to the time you were arrested, had you been performing military duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to that, well I was, but maybe it was one month prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the people were being searched in the hangar, was anyone mistreated, that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. While they were taking us into the hangar, one of us did not raise his hands on time and then the soldier hit him a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the man who was hit, do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zakir Bulut. He was hit by Anto Kristo. He used to go to school with me, that is how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you had been through this process, were there any other people brought into the hangar that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, people from another village were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these people Muslims too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What village were they brought from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the village of Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they processed in a similar way to the way you had been processed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Whoever was brought in, that way -- has to go through the same procedure as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you spend the whole night in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the concrete floor, there was nothing on the floor, on the floor of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any heating in the hangar that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened on the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every day new people were brought in from various locations and then a few days later three more persons were brought in from the Osmancevic family, but they did not stay there very long. We were there until we were taken out for digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When -- you mentioned that incident of the Osmancevic family. Can you go into some more detail about that? Who brought them in and who was there when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were simply thrown into the hangar and maybe an hour later a military policeman came with the warden and another person, whose name I do not know, and they were simply taken away and we have not heard anything about them, to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned the warden. Who was the warden that came with the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also mentioned being taken to the trenches to dig trenches, or dig. Where were you taken? What were the names of the places you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Ahmici, Loncari, Jelinak, Kula and Podjele locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taken to these locations, who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken by HVO soldiers, who were there at those lines. They would come up and select a certain number of people and they would take us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any guards or officials from the camp on hand when you were selected to be taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there would always be a guard and the warden would sometimes be there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, just for the record, when you say "warden", who do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was any record kept of the people that were taken for trench digging, that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a soldier who was in charge of keeping some kind of record. He would always draw up a list of persons who were supposed to go to various locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was that soldier, so far as you could ascertain, part of the camp administration or a soldier from outside the camp, that you could tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that he was from the administration, most probably so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I wonder if you would do something for me. I will show you a map and on that map I would ask you to mark for me in a highlighter pen the places that you mentioned that you were taken to for trench digging. I have copies for your Honours, whether your Honours need it or not, I am not sure because it is the same map that has been produced. Perhaps the copy that is shown to the witness might be given the next exhibit number in order of the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness E, would you please study the map for a moment that is in front of you there. We then want to put it on to the screen beside you. With the highlighter pen, I would like you to go through and mark the places that you can remember that you were taken to for trench digging. Can you do that for me? Do it on the actual video machine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you mark it, tell us which ones you are marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map). Do you want me to encircle the location?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fine. Put a circle around it, that would be fine. What is that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Kula. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ahmici, Jelinak, Loncari, Podjele. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, your Honour, that exhibit. I would now like to show the witness another map -- another photograph, if I may. Perhaps it could given the next number in order. Your Honours, there is a copy of this for your Honours and for the Defence. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness E, have a look and study this photograph for me again, if you would, please. Tell me, by looking at it, if you can recognise what it is a photograph of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depicts locations around the camp where we were taken to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you, firstly -- are you able to, putting that on the projector again, if you would do that for me, with your pen, could you mark the location of the camp? On this occasion I would like if you would give it the letter "A", the camp site. On that photograph, can you mark the camp site with the letter "A" on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is excellent, thank you. Now, by looking at that photograph, are you able to see any places that you were taken to to dig trenches? If you can see those places, the places where you had to dig trenches, could you, again, draw a circle for us? Would you tell us the name of the place, then we will give it the next alphabetical letter, "B", for the next one? Would you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is that that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Podjele.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next one: what is that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Jelinak, "C". "D" for Loncari. (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that, your Honours. I think that is all there is on that photograph. Apart from having to go out and work outside of the camp digging trenches, were there any other duties that you had to perform outside of the camp during the period of your imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Podjele several times. We did some work on the bridge there. Those were wooden bridges and had to be cemented. We also went to do agricultural work for several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is fine. I would like you to look at the next photograph, if you would, for me, please. Again, it is a more expanded version of the photograph we just looked at. (Handed). Again, there is a copies for your Honour, and one for the Defence. Might it be awarded the next Prosecution number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just study that for a moment, if you would, for me, please, Witness E. I would like you, if you would, to mark on it -- if you can see it there -- the Kaonik camp. Perhaps you might put a circle around the Kaonik camp, then a letter "A". And the place in Podjele where you had to work on the bridges. If you mark that and put a letter "B".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the Kaonik camp, it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you put a circle around the location at Podjele where you had to repair the bridges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marked map).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that could be marked with a "B".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We worked on one more locality a little further off. I do not think you can see it on this map, but somewhere around here, up here. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will leave that one for the minute. Thank you. We will leave that to be tendered into evidence, if your Honours please. You mentioned going to Ahmici. When you went to Ahmici, who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A member of the HVO came and later we were told that his name is Cisko. He selected 20 of us, in the presence of Zlatko Aleksovski, and he took us to the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to the village of Ahmici, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The houses were still aflame. There was nobody there. Everything was burnt or burning. There were several animals that had been killed lying around, slaughtered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this person that you later came to know as Cisko, did he say anything to you when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we got to the place where we were supposed to dig the trenches, he told us that if anybody tried to escape -- and he took out a huge knife which was still covered in blood -- and he said: "If anybody tries to escape, he will be killed in the same way the children in Ahmici were killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you have to stay there digging trenches that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there the whole night, until the morning and then were taken back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How many people were in the hangar in the time that you were kept there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 200 to 300, and later on more people were brought in from Travnik and other places, people we did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the conditions in the hangar in terms of what you were given to eat and the sanitary conditions and sleeping conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sleeping conditions; there were some pallets, wooden pallets. Later on we brought these into the hangar and lay on them. As far as food is concerned, at the beginning they would give us one to two loaves of bread per 100/200 people and we had to go to the toilet in the hangar in a sort of larger bucket, latrine or bucket.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of Cisko taking you to Ahmici. Were you taken to other locations by Cisko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on he selected a group of 20 of us, above the village of Loncari. We started -- we had already started digging, but he lined us up into two columns and he said: "Anybody who comes under me, who is a Muslim, will have to learn to make the sign of the cross first, that is a rule with me." After that, as he recognised one of his co-workers from his company, he told him to step out and show us how to do this. He stepped out, he did not know how to make the sign of the cross and he was told how to do this. When he did it, we stepped out one by one and had to make the sign of the cross ourselves, after which we returned to our digging jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, were you able to gain a sense of how close you were to the front-lines while you were digging these trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, let us say about 100 to 200 metres. Two to three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was there any fighting or military activity going on at the time when you were out digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, while I was there, there was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you always kept in the hangar or were you later moved somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, when they took us out, say one month later, the ones that remained in the hangar, they took us out, and the elderly, and they sent us to the village of Skradno and we were under house arrest. There was 18 of us and we were then transferred to the hangar with the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the hangar with the cells, do you know who was being kept there or some of the people being kept there? Not necessarily by name, but perhaps by description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In one of the cells I knew some of the people and we would meet in the lavatories from time to time. There were 11 Arabs. In a solitary confinement cell there was a man from Travnik and some others, probably one of their soldiers. He was in this solitary confinement cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were there, did anything happen to these 11 Arab people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were often -- often cries were heard coming from the cell. They were maltreated, they were beaten. You could hear this noise coming from the cells and the man in the solitary confinement cell we could hear similar noises coming from that cell too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who was doing these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How often did they occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically all the time. HVO soldiers or some of the staff would go -- every day we would hear this, every day people would be beaten up, almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you ever addressed by the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning he said: "I am the commander. Everything that you need, there will not be any problems ..." and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you, at any stage, registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the 19th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of the two hangars, the first one that you went to, then the cell block. I ask you to look at the photograph I am now going to show you. I ask you if you recognise the photograph. We have photocopies of the photographs, your Honours. Hopefully in due course we will be able to replace those with actual prints. At this stage we only have photocopies and I apologise for that, your Honours. Likewise with Mr. Mikulicic, we will provide him with copies. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be placed -- once you have looked on it -- on the overhead projector. Again, with the pointer, can you point out with the pointer what it is that you know about this photograph that you could draw our attention to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This hangar here is where we are for the first month. We were later on transferred to this second hangar with the cells. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first hangar indicated by the witness is the shown in the foreground of the photograph, it is the largest building appearing in the foreground to the right-hand side of the photograph. The building more distant pointed to by the witness on the left-hand side of the photograph, the witness described as the building with the cells. Are these two places contained within the Kaonik camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph. I have another photograph I would like you to look at for me, if you would. Again, your Honours, we have a copy. (Handed). If it could be given the next number, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the hangar with the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Looking at that photograph now, can you point to the entry to the cells, the main entry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And on the -- there is what appears to be two windows on either side of the entry that you have just pointed to. Do you know what rooms those windows go into?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the left-hand side was the warden's office. On the right-hand side were the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And by "the warden", who do you mean, just for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were the cells, did they have any windows that you can point to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cells were to the right, three to the right. (Indicating on photograph). Then across the hall on this side, there were three more. Then they would stretch along the left-hand side. I am not quite sure how many. Three here, two toilets there, and three cells along here. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender that photograph, your Honours. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P20? (Handed). Just looking at that photograph, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This -- in this room, this is where the guards were, with the bars on the windows. These are the three cells. I was in this one here, cell 16, 15 and 14. Across the hallway was cell number 11, which were the villagers of Loncari. This is the table where we had our meals. (Indicating on photograph).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. If that could be returned to the Registrar, I would be grateful. During the time that you were held captive in the Kaonik camp, did you loose any weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about 42/43 kilos was my weight when I was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the sanitary conditions like in terms of being able to shower and bath and so forth during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in the camp, more than two months, I never had a chance of taking a shower. I never took a shower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am going to now ask the witness to describe an event, where he may mention names of people who have previously been assigned pseudonyms. For that reason, may we go into private session, while the witness describes this event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, would you object to that or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. We are now in a private session then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you released from the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released on the 19th June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you released in a group or were you on your own? Can you just describe the circumstances of your release?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a group of us with the guard. I do not remember his name. We were harvesting the grass and they said he had an important piece of news for us and he told us that there would be an exchange in the afternoon and that we could go home. That is exactly what happened. The Red Cross came and their HVO soldiers from Zenica were brought and then we were released, all of us except one Arab person who remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just going back to the time when you were in the camp, the guards that were in the camp, the camp guards as opposed to soldiers in the field, can you recall how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you notice any markings or insignia on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, how much time do you think you might need for your cross-examination? Because we cannot go beyond 1.15 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will have quite a few questions for this witness, so with the court's indulgence, I propose that we wind up today, so that I do not interrupt my cross-examination. I would like to begin my cross-examination tomorrow. That would be my application, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you like to say anything on that score?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, the only point I make is that we have Professor Biancini who will testify tomorrow. I expect -- I had planned his evidence would probably take all the morning, but it may not. We may be able to do both. That was the only consideration I had. 15 minutes is not much time, so I am not wanting to press Mr. Mikulicic, if he feels he would prefer not to interrupt his cross-examination. I just indicate that it may have the consequence that we do not completely finish Professor Bijancini. We will have to see. That is as best as I can put the it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So then, perhaps we should take account of what the counsel for the accused has said. We will give due time to the Defence. After that tomorrow, we will be hearing the Professor. We will leave it there for today. We would like to thank you, Witness E, for having testified before this Tribunal. If the usher would be so good as to bring down the blinds. See you all tomorrow then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: on Thursday, 26th February 1998)
